summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an interactive web platform built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (Planet X and SPHEREx) to visualize multi-epoch, near-infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission (0.75–5.0 µm) and help users detect celestial motion and variability over time.
Instead of downloading massive all-sky FITS archives in the browser, our architecture pairs an offline Python scientific preparation pipeline (ZScale/Asinh contrast stretching, quality masking, WCS reprojection, and WebP cutout export) with a fast, responsive React/TypeScript explorer and FastAPI backend. Users can scrub temporal timelines, switch between single-epoch, buildup, and stacked views for targets like Comet 3I/ATLAS and Asteroid 4 Vesta, inspect differences using blink, side-by-side, and image-subtraction viewers, toggle dark/light themes, follow an interactive guided tour, and download frames for further analysis.
By making SPHEREx spectral time-series data intuitive and browser-accessible, SPHEREx Sky Explorer empowers researchers, students, and citizen scientists to spot moving solar system bodies and candidate Planet X signals without specialized astronomy software.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an interactive web application built to visualize multi-epoch, near-infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx mission (0.75–5.0 µm) and make it easy to spot moving celestial bodies and brightness changes over time.

It works across two decoupled tiers:

  1. Offline Scientific Preparation Pipeline (science/ & scripts/): Instead of streaming gigabytes of raw FITS files to users, the Python pipeline queries observation metadata first (IRSA TAP/SIA cutout architecture), extracts small target-centered cutouts, masks unusable quality flags, subtracts zodiacal background light, reprojects multi-epoch cutouts onto a common World Coordinate System (WCS), applies ZScale + Asinh contrast stretching, and exports lightweight 8-bit WebP frames paired with index.json provenance manifests.
  2. Interactive Browser Explorer (src/, apps/web/, services/api/): A responsive React/TypeScript frontend (backed by FastAPI and static frame hosting) loads target catalogs—including Comet 3I/ATLAS, Asteroid 4 Vesta, and test fields—and provides:
    • Temporal Timeline: Frame scrubber, play/pause animation with adjustable FPS, and automatic frame preloading.
    • Unified Target & Product Views: Seamless switching between single-epoch, cumulative buildup, and stacked views for moving targets rather than cluttering the catalog with duplicate entries.
    • Comparison Studio: Blink comparator (alternating two epochs at configurable intervals), Side-by-Side view with synchronized pan and zoom, and real-time client-side Difference imaging (HTML5 Canvas pixel subtraction with adjustable gain and color modes).
    • Science Context & Export: Spectral Wavelength Badge (0.75–5.0 µm detector band info), "What am I looking at?" Explainer Panel, optional target/predicted-position overlays, one-click image downloads across viewers, an interactive Guided Tour, and a persistent Dark/Light theme toggle (defaulting to dark).

Benefits

  • Zero-Barrier Access: Anyone can inspect infrared time-series cutouts directly in a desktop or mobile browser—no local FITS software or astronomy toolchain required.
  • Fast, Low-Bandwidth Performance: Heavy WCS alignment and contrast stretching happen offline once; browsers only load compact WebP frames and lightweight JSON metadata.
  • Full Scientific Provenance: Every displayed frame preserves its obs_id, UTC timestamp, RA/Dec coordinates, central wavelength (µm), and SPHEREx detector array (D1–D6).
  • Actionable Outputs: Users can download individual frames, comparison views, or difference maps directly for reports, classrooms, or follow-up study.

Intended Impact

By lowering the technical barrier to inspecting NASA’s all-sky near-infrared spectral survey, SPHEREx Sky Explorer empowers citizen scientists, students, educators, and researchers to visually explore multi-epoch sky changes—supporting discovery and validation of moving solar system objects (comets, asteroids, interstellar visitors like 3I/ATLAS), transient phenomena, and distant Planet X candidates.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS v4, TanStack React Query, Lucide React, HTML5 Canvas API (real-time difference imaging & image export).
  • Backend & Science Pipeline: Python 3.10+, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn, Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, NumPy, SciPy, Reproject, Pillow, Matplotlib, Pytest.
  • Deployment & Infrastructure: Node.js, Bun/npm, GitHub Pages (remote frame dataset hosting), Vercel Services (multi-service Vite + FastAPI deployment).
  • Hardware: Standard consumer laptops/desktops and mobile devices—decoupling FITS processing offline means the live explorer runs smoothly without specialized client hardware or GPUs.

How the Project Is Creative

  • Browser-Based Blink & Subtraction Studio: Brings classic astronomical discovery techniques—blink comparison, synchronized dual-epoch zooming, and gain-tuned difference imaging—into a fast, zero-install web interface using HTML5 Canvas.
  • Unified Multi-Mode Target Exploration: Groups normal, buildup, and stacked exposures under a single target entry so users can effortlessly compare frame-by-frame motion against deep stacked baselines.
  • Onboarding Built Into the Science Workflow: An interactive spotlight Guided Tour walks first-time visitors step by step through target selection, timeline playback, comparison/difference modes, and exporting discovery images.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Data Scale & Bandwidth: Avoiding full-sky downloads in favor of small spatial cutouts, WebP compression, and CORS-safe proxy fallbacks (/remote-frames/).
  • Deterministic Science First: Prioritizing classical, reproducible astronomical processing (quality masking, zodi subtraction, WCS reprojection, ZScale/Asinh stretch) and strict provenance tracking before applying machine learning.
  • Accessibility & Mobile Ergonomics: High-contrast dark-room default with light-mode persistence, visible keyboard focus rings, prefers-reduced-motion compliance (preventing unwanted auto-play), minimum 44px touch targets, pinch-to-zoom, and a mobile drawer/bottom navigation bar below 900px.
  • Deployment Reliability: Structuring the repository with clean separation between offline data prep (science/), API serving (services/api/), and frontend delivery (vercel.json multi-service routing) so both local development and cloud deployment run cleanly.
